title: Certified measurement and control of an entanglement-breaking index on programmable hardware
abstract: The entanglement-breaking index of a quantum channel, the number of self-compositions after which the channel destroys all entanglement with any reference, has to our knowledge never been measured. We show that a certified thermal collision feedback loop makes this integer both measurable and controllable on current programmable hardware, every load-bearing quantity delivered as an interval-arithmetic certificate. On the measurement side: a target list for the integer staircase n_EB(p) with decision-point negativities certified at margins 0.025 to 0.109; an exact per-round depolarising model in which the selected staircase survives realistic noise as certified integers; an exact, tight compilation of the round unitary (seven CNOTs all-to-all, five native arbitrary-angle gates, ten on heavy-hex); and a 33-million-draw gated search bounding the thermal valley's contrast by a wall with an interior maximum, a certified 2.85x10^-3 near floor 89. On the control side: the model composes rounds of differing bath polarisation exactly, so the valley becomes a pulsed valve, switching at a certified minimal pulse of exactly eight rounds; the optimal pulsed signal, a certified 3.43x10^-3, beats the static protocol, so the best valley measurement is intrinsically pulsed; and a coherent tilt of the bath Bloch vector lifts the signal to a certified 8.6x10^-3, three times the static ceiling, at zero population cost. Valley signatures certifiably die near per-round noise strength 10^-4, fixing the error-extrapolation burden. The staircase is a near-term experiment; the pulsed valley a precisely priced one.
summary: This work introduces a method to certify the measurement and control of the entanglement-breaking index of a quantum channel on programmable hardware. By utilizing a thermal collision feedback loop, the authors demonstrate that pulsed operations and coherent field tilts can significantly enhance the measurable signal compared to static protocols. The entire framework is underpinned by rigorous mathematical certification using advanced interval arithmetic.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of measuring and controlling the entanglement-breaking index, $n_{EB}(\Phi)$, of a quantum channel, an index previously unmeasurable.
main_result: They demonstrate that this index can be certified as measurable and controllable on current programmable hardware using a thermal collision feedback loop, achieving improvements via pulsed operations and coherent control.
method: The methodology relies heavily on rigorous mathematical certification using ball arithmetic (256 bits) to establish bounds on observables like negativity, combined with experimental simulation techniques like gated search and circuit compilation.
model_or_system: The system models a quantum channel $\Phi$ acting on a message qubit, whose properties are controlled by varying the bath polarization $p$ via a collision feedback loop. The process is simulated on programmable hardware using specific unitary gates (CNOTs, arbitrary-angle gates).
key_observables: Entanglement-breaking index ($n_{EB}$), Negativity, Bath Polarization ($p$), and the contrast of the 'thermal valley'.
important_parameters: Noise strength ($\lambda$), decision-point margins (0.025 to 0.109), and the number of rounds/pulse depth (e.g., 53 rounds).
main_assumptions: The certification relies on exact arithmetic in ball arithmetic, and the measured index is only a lower bound due to hardware noise.
figures_summary: The notes reference tables detailing objective targets for the staircase measurement and comparisons between pulsed, static, and coherently tilted signal strengths.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the unmeasurable index to proposing a measurable protocol using a collision feedback loop. It details measurement techniques (staircase, noise resilience), control mechanisms (pulsing, coherent tilt), and concludes with the quantitative results demonstrating the superiority of pulsed/coherent methods.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of certified computation techniques (ball arithmetic) to a fundamental quantum information measure like $n_{EB}$ provides a powerful blueprint for verifying complex quantum properties on near-term hardware.
